"Implement the solution in robot_name.cpp, robot_name.h so that the tests in robot_name_test.cpp pass. The specification follows.

# Instructions

Manage robot factory settings.

When a robot comes off the factory floor, it has no name.

The first time you turn on a robot, a random name is generated in the format of two uppercase letters followed by three digits, such as RX837 or BC811.

Every once in a while we need to reset a robot to its factory settings, which means that its name gets wiped.
The next time you ask, that robot will respond with a new random name.

The names must be random: they should not follow a predictable sequence.
Using random names means a risk of collisions.
Your solution must ensure that every existing robot has a unique name.


Do NOT modify the tests or the build files except as stated below. Do not create new files unless the specification requires them; Helper .h / .cpp files may go beside the solution."

Done. Let me summarize the solution.

All 5 test cases pass (2004 assertions). The solution:

**`robot_name.h`** — declares a `robot` class with `std::string name() const` and `void reset()`, storing the current name in a private member.

**`robot_name.cpp`** — implements the logic:
- `generate_name()` builds a random name (two uppercase letters + three digits) using a `std::mt19937` engine seeded from `std::random_device`, so names don't follow a predictable sequence.
- `unique_name()` keeps a static `std::unordered_set` of every name ever handed out and retries generation until it finds one not in that set, guarded by a mutex — guaranteeing every existing robot has a unique name, even after resets.
- The constructor assigns a unique name, `name()` returns the stored name (stable across calls), and `reset()` replaces it with a fresh unique one.

The code compiles cleanly under `-Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror` with C++17, and the full suite (`EXERCISM_RUN_ALL_TESTS`) passes: `All tests passed (2004 assertions in 5 test cases)`.
